I was sorta on the fence about firearm ownership, and then I got my first handgun. We now have three in the house and I'm a daily conceal carrier. Probably won't ever have to use it, but if I do, I'll be ready to. I'd like to give you some specific advice, with a little explanation as to why I think it'll help.

  • Don't just buy a gun and go to the range with it alone. Many things that are dangerous to do with guns don't look or feel dangerous on instinct--a lot of safe gun handling is learning how to be pedantic, and safety focused to the point of obsession.

  • Watch YouTube videos about how to safely handle a gun at the range. This will get you used to the sorts of things you're likely to hear when you go for training and to handle a real gun. It's a good idea to have some exposure ahead of time, so that the things you hear at the range aren't confusing and brand-new.

  • Find a range near your house, and ask them what you can do to prepare to shoot a gun for the first time at their range. Most ranges will either run an introductory course, where they provide a gun and ammunition to you if you don't have your own to bring (or will help you handle your gun if you do have one to bring and are unfamiliar with it). Getting a friend or family member to take you to the range is good too, but be very sure that you're listening to somebody that emphasizes real safety--learning bad habits from an experienced person can be more dangerous than having no guidance at all!!

It's not a bad idea to go to a range where you can rent handguns at a low price and try several different ones to see what works best for you. This is a nice way to spend a moderate amount of money, but to know for sure when you commit to a wait time, a federal transfer form, and a $500 to $1,500 purchase, you're getting something you like.

Personally, I'm a big glock fan, especially for beginners. The design is ergonomic, simple, and they have fantastic safety against accidental fire pitfalls like drop-firing. Additionally, I'm not a big fan of safeties--someday, between the day you buy that gun and the day you die, that safety's not gonna be in the position you think it is. You're either gonna need to fire to save your life, and your gun won't fire--or you're treating a gun like it can't fire, but a pull on the trigger would end in disaster. Either way, the Glock's approach of, "If there's one in the chamber, the trigger is hot" design, combined with the intricate mechanical safeties and legendary reliability even after being maintained very poorly, make it a solid choice for a tool you want to protect your life with if need be.
